title: Your first scene
summary: Build a scene, add a shape, and compose its appearance, movement and exit with awaited animations.
outcome: A circle that appears, moves across the canvas and fades out.

blocks.text: A Scene is a script and local entity graph. Its constructor does not create a GPU device. `start(canvas)` creates and attaches a composer when needed and launches `run()`. Place GPU-dependent setup inside `run()`, where the scene has a device, renderer and camera.

items: The circle’s geometry is created in local space; moving the entity changes its transform.

`this.add(circle)` establishes scene ownership. `play()` also registers the roots of entities referenced by recognized animations, but explicit ownership makes composite scenes easier to reason about.
Each awaited play waits for its animations to resolve. Passing several targets to one play runs them together.
Durations and wait values are milliseconds. The position uses arbitrary world units chosen to match the camera.
`FadeOut` changes appearance; visibility, scene attachment and GPU lifetime are separate concerns. Use the explicit removal or cleanup API when the object is no longer needed.
Change radius from 1 to 1.8, then change the camera’s orthoScale to 16.
Replace easeInOutCubic with linear to compare timing.
Pass two circles’ animators to one play to see concurrency.
Turn off Preserve State before rerunning when you want the camera and timeline to start from scratch.

blocks.text: In an external npm project, save the scene with explicit retiam imports and a default class export. Use the [installation host](/installation#create-a-consumer-application) to preview it and select it for CLI rendering. The documentation runs the same kind of scene through a CDN-loaded engine; your project resolves the installed npm package.

Once the scene looks right, continue with [video rendering](/export#cli-preview-and-final-render). Use [independent scene export](/export#standalone-embeds) when the result should remain interactive on another website.
Follow the guides in order using Previous and Next, or browse [Tutorials](/tutorials) for a practical lesson.
